nodes.label: Raw-data buffer / staging layer (decided 2026-06-18, Leo). Raw

data.statement: - **Raw-data buffer / staging layer (decided 2026-06-18, Leo).** Raw ingested data lands in a **raw/staging buffer** — object storage, **parquet** (the bronze layer) — and **dehydration happens from there**. The raw/parquet layer is where analytical processing runs: **Glue (AWS) / Azure equivalent** (Synapse / Data Lake Analytics) over the parquet. **Cross-store erasure must propagate across all layers**: ingest -> raw/staging buffer -> dehydrated -> CDP. Cloud-portable: raw parquet in object storage is portable; the query engine over it is cloud-specific but swappable (Glue is AWS-only — not in scope if Azure; use the Azure equivalent).

- **Data-lifecycle / dehydration mechanism: time-partition + rotate out (decided 2026-06-18, Leo).** Append-only and observation tables (the consent ledger, the `event` time spine, identity/attribute history) are **range-partitioned by time (year/month)**. Old partitions rotate to the **dehydrated tier** — detach + archive to cold object storage (S3 / Azure Blob) — and **re-hydrate on demand** (re-attach/restore). Realizes the `active -> raw -> archived -> dehydrated -> erasure` lifecycle (`11-tiered-data-lifecycle.md`). Cloud-portable: Postgres native declarative partitioning + object storage, no proprietary service. Keeps hot tables small without losing history.

- **Field Catalog v1 prioritization — LOCKED 2026-06-19 (Alicia Salazar).** 14 of 27 fields are **valuable-now** (Phase 1 build target); 13 are **interesting-later** (Phase 2+). (The lock enumerated 14 valuable-now fields; the original "13" headline was a miscount of the enumerated list — corrected 2026-06-21.) Valuable-now: fields 1–7, 9–11, 13, 15, 23, 24 — identity/vehicle/purchase core (name, email, phone, VIN, year/make/model, purchase date), mileage (at-sale snapshot), vehicle condition (derived from deal type), completed services (validate DMS feed), equity + market value (BlackBook). Interesting-later: trim level (partial dealer coverage), purchase price (dealer access unconfirmed), declined services (messy ETL), open recalls (RecallMasters — new vendor integration), OEM maintenance schedule, completed recalls, services w/ media, service coupons, service/warranty plan offerings, upgrade options, insurance provider + quotes (no source today). Full table in `docs/cdp-field-source-matrix.md` (Phase column).

nodes.label: Cross-store erasure orchestration: Temporal workflow saga

data.statement: - **Cross-store erasure orchestration: Temporal workflow saga — APPROVED 2026-06-19 (Alicia, Privacy-by-Design).** Full crypto-shred saga runs as a single durable Temporal workflow: destroy DEK (DynamoDB) → evict plaintext DEK (Redis) → purge Postgres → purge S3 bronze → purge Redshift → purge OpenSearch → write erasure audit. Built-in retries, idempotency, single auditable completion record. Temporal already in stack as app-layer orchestrator. Same workflow covers key rotation and re-encryption. See `docs/consent-pii-erasure-options.md` Option C2. - **Mechanism superseded 2026-06-21 (Leo) — orchestration approval stands.** The saga's underlying mechanism is no longer crypto-shred / per-consumer DEK; it now drives the PII-vault row delete (see next bullet). The Temporal orchestration pattern Alicia approved is unchanged — only the first step changes (delete deletable vault rows + write tombstone → confirm tokens dereference to nothing across stores → write audit). The DynamoDB DEK-store / Redis DEK-cache / per-store PII purge steps drop away, because PII lives only in the vault. The mechanism change was shared with Alicia + Luis on 2026-06-21 as a **heads-up (informational, not a gate)**; the decision stands and any feedback is incorporated when it arrives.

nodes.label: PII erasure mechanism: tokenized reference vault + delete-the-

data.statement: - **PII erasure mechanism: tokenized reference vault + delete-the-row — DECIDED 2026-06-21 (Leo), supersedes per-consumer DEK / crypto-shred (`docs/consent-pii-erasure-options.md` Option set A).** Per-person encryption keys are rejected: too complex, brittle, and expensive (10M+ wrapped-key rows, decrypt-on-every-read + isolated DEK cache infra, cache-coherence and accidental-erasure risk, and the GLBA partial-deletion key-granularity problem). Instead: identity-class PII (name / email / phone / address) is centralized in a single mutable **PII vault** keyed by a surrogate token; the append-only observation/event log, bronze parquet, analytics, and OpenSearch store **tokens + non-PII provenance only, never raw values**. Erasure = delete/null the vault row(s) — tokens elsewhere dereference to nothing, so there is **no cross-store PII purge to propagate** (also removes the Redshift-specific propagation problem; analytics stays Postgres-centric/portable per the Azure-primary / portable-OSS-core stance). **Provenance/lineage for PII is retained** (Leo's explicit requirement): the observation log keeps which source supplied each field, when, and by what method, referencing the value by token — erasing the value leaves "phone provided by DMS on 2026-01-01 via batch" intact. **Scoped GLBA / legal-hold deletion** is plain row selection on source + purpose (no sub-keys; dissolves the prior open key-granularity decision). **Backups** age out by retention policy, not fast purge — deletion policy means not-retained-forever, not delete-immediately. **Optional defense-in-depth (feature-flagged, per-record, off by default):** per-row salt (stored in the row) + a single external pepper (secrets manager) derive a per-row protection key via KDF — DB-dump / backup protection with one secret, not per-person keys; a per-row scheme marker lets plaintext and hardened rows coexist and the flag flip on/off without schema change; hardened-row ciphertext is intentionally non-matchable (matching is on normalized tokens in the identity graph); pepper / derived keys may be cached in an isolated Redis (short TTL, separate from app cache, evicts on erasure) to avoid a secrets/DB round-trip per decryption. **Pepper-clear** is a coarse kill-switch: clearing the pepper makes every value derived from it unreadable at once — global, or per-tenant if the pepper is scoped per tenant (leaning per-tenant for clean dealer offboarding); all-or-nothing, ignores legal holds, so for decommission / offboard / breach only. **Decided 2026-06-21:** pepper scope is **per-tenant by default**, configurable to global (a setting resolved via the policy-config layer). The **policy values** (retention periods, consent taxonomy, lawful basis, suppression scope) are populated by Alicia + Luis; DAS Legal is not a Phase-0 blocker — they approve the proposal once authored. Documented in `wiki/Privacy-by-Design.md`. - **Ingest tokenization boundary — tokenize at the CDP, not at the edge (2026-06-21, Leo).** Identity is resolved *inside* the CDP; source systems and the ingest edge carry fragmented single-vector views (much lower re-identification risk — risk concentrates at resolution). Tokenize on ingest **into the CDP only** — extract PII to the vault, leave tokens in the CDP's own stores (observation log, golden record, analytics, search). Do **not** put a tokenization barrier in front of **block storage or event processing** — excessive decentralized coordination on the hottest paths for little benefit on already-fragmented data. Three zones: (1) ingest edge — event bus/stream + raw bronze parquet landing, raw + fragmented, governed by bounded retention/age-out + access control, no per-request delete propagation; (2) CDP boundary — tokenize on ingest; (3) CDP resolved layer — vault holds raw PII, everything else holds tokens, erasure honored here by vault-row delete. Deletion posture: precise delete where identity is concentrated (CDP), retention/age-out where data is fragmented (edge). Honest caveat: a raw edge fragment (e.g. raw email in bronze during its retention window) is still PII under CCPA/TDPSA — defensible via bounded edge retention + fragmentation + access control + precise resolved-record deletion (same shape as backup age-out); DAS Legal approves at proposal stage, not a Phase-0 blocker; per-source edge tokenization can be enabled via the policy-config layer for high-sensitivity sources. - **Offer both mechanisms; vault is default (2026-06-21, Leo).** We can present both crypto-shred and vault; vault (delete-the-row) is the default/recommendation. Crypto-shred stays available where a source/contract demands cryptographic erasure, but its decentralized coordinated cross-store delete is **excessive for this architecture** (centralizing PII removes the scattered-PII condition it solves). Offering both is a per-scope policy choice, not two parallel builds. - **Resolver blocking-key boundary (2026-06-21, Leo).** The `person` shell carries pseudonymous one-way blocking keys (email/phone hashes, metaphone, zip) *outside* the vault because deterministic matching needs them queryable. They are not vault PII, but they are a re-identification path — so **erasure scrubs the email/phone hashes** alongside the vault delete; the `person_id` shell + tokenized history remain for bitemporal integrity. Acceptable boundary. - **Policy-config layer needed (raised 2026-06-21, Leo; spec TBD).** The salt+pepper toggle — and retention, tiering, suppression scope, edge-tokenization — are configurable per **source / channel / partner / dealership / user**. A single record matches several scopes at once, so a policy-config layer with deterministic resolution is required (most-restrictive-wins for protection/retention obligations, regulatory floor non-overridable; explicit per-scope settings). We build the config layer + resolver + admin surface; Alicia + Luis + Legal populate the policy values. Candidate spec: `specs/03-phase-1-build/03-backend-data-model/18-policy-config-layer.md` (next free number).

- **Consent-ledger mechanism: portable, application-built, append-only hash-chained (decided 2026-06-18, Leo).** The consent/suppression ledger is built in-application (SHA-256 hash chain), **cloud-portable** — deploys identically on Azure AKS or AWS EKS, no cloud-KMS-specific signing (avoids coupling to AWS KMS / Azure Key Vault). Any signing uses a portable mechanism (app-held key / HMAC). Consistent with the portable-OSS-core / Azure-or-AWS stance; the same portability principle extends to crypto-shred key management (cloud-agnostic KMS abstraction, not a specific cloud KMS). Resolves the consent-ledger open question (1 of 4 open consent-enforcement items); the policy layer, cross-store erasure orchestration, and event-sourced-artifact access remain with the Privacy-by-Design deliverable (Alicia + Luis).

nodes.label: Language strategy (2026-06-14): Python primary, Go for perform

data.statement: - **Language strategy (2026-06-14): Python primary, Go for performance-critical systems.** Python is the broad default — Django API, Airflow/Temporal workers, resolver and transform logic — one ecosystem shared with the Python ingestion stack. Go is reserved for performance-sensitive components (high-throughput event/ingest hot paths) where measured need warrants it. - *Rationale (thought process, documented for the team as Phase 0 wraps):* Python is the strongest ecosystem for the work that dominates this build — AI/agentic tooling and ML (identity resolution, LLM features, reuse of DAS's AI layer at `ai.das-technology.com`) and general cloud/glue — and it unifies with the Airflow ingestion stack, so one team and one toolchain span ingest + API + resolver. Go is the deliberate exception for hot paths where Python's throughput ceiling bites (event intake fan-in, high-QPS serving), kept narrow to avoid polyglot sprawl. - *Why not — alternatives considered (the deciding factor is ecosystem gravity toward data/AI + cohesion with the Python ingestion stack, NOT web-framework productivity, where the alternatives below are all capable web stacks):* - **Node.js / TypeScript** — this was DAS's own v3/v4 proposal (Express API + Node event workers + ONNX-in-Node ML serving + Next.js, on Azure AKS). Strong for I/O-bound APIs, good typing, shared types with the Next.js frontend. Rejected for the BACKEND only (we keep Next.js/TypeScript on the frontend — TS is not banned): this build's center of gravity is AI/ML identity resolution and data engineering, which is Python-native — the v3 plan itself trains models in Python and bridges them into Node via ONNX, a seam we remove by being Python end-to-end (training, serving, resolver, batch on one runtime). Node's ML/data ecosystem is thin (no pandas/scikit/xgboost-native/feature-tooling parity), CPU-bound resolution/embedding/batch work fights its single-threaded event loop, and an Express backend is assemble-your-own (Drizzle + bolt-on migrations) vs Django's batteries-included ORM/migrations/admin. Choosing Node for the API reintroduces the Python(ML/data) + Node(API) split — the exact seam we eliminate. We keep the strong parts of v3: Next.js frontend, Postgres + RLS, AKS-portability, and the tiered AI resolution design. - **Spring Boot (Java/JVM)** — strong typing, performance, mature enterprise tooling. Rejected: migrations are a bolt-on (Flyway/Liquibase) not batteries-included, GraphQL less native, more ceremony for CRUD+resolver work, and — decisive — it splits the runtime from our Python ingestion (Airflow/Temporal) and the AI/ML ecosystem, doubling the operational and staffing surface for no offsetting gain at our scale. - **Rails (Ruby)** — a genuine peer to Django on the web/API side (productive, great migrations, batteries-included). Rejected on ecosystem, not web merits: Ruby is weak for the AI/ML and data-engineering work that dominates this build and would not unify with Airflow/Temporal/resolver tooling — choosing it means Ruby for the API and Python for everything data/AI, exactly the split we avoid by standardizing on Django. Smaller talent overlap with the data/ML side. - **PHP / Laravel** — fast CRUD, polished full-stack framework, solid Eloquent ORM + migrations. Rejected: weakest fit for a data-/AI-centric platform — effectively no serious ML/AI/data-engineering ecosystem, request-response heritage is a poor fit for long-running workers / streaming / identity-resolution sagas, weak concurrency/compute story vs Python+Go, and zero cohesion with the Python data stack. This is a data platform with a web API on top, not a web app.

nodes.label: Deletion strategy: two-stage soft-then-hard. Dan: soft delete

source.locator: Client-confirmed 2026-06-17 (Dan Aston, Teams chat — open-item reconciliation; DAS spot-checking gaps to inform design/product strategy, more questions incoming)

data.statement: - **Deletion strategy: two-stage soft-then-hard.** Dan: soft delete first (move the record to an "old store"), then a hard delete (expunge) after. DAS has NO existing standard — "now is a time we can do that" — so the CDP defines it, no legacy constraint. Reconcile with append-only/bitemporal: our mechanism is crypto-shred (destroy per-consumer DEK → PII unreadable, structure stays — `docs/consent-pii-erasure-options.md` Option A). Map soft→old-store→hard-delete onto crypto-shred + cross-store purge (Option C orchestration) and set the retention window for the soft/old-store stage. **Refined 2026-06-17 — tiered data lifecycle:** not two stages but tiers — active records -> raw data -> archival -> dehydrated (lower-tier/cold storage) -> erasure — configurable by policy, **per source and per core entity**. Cold data relocates to cheaper storage (S3 IA/Glacier, Blob Cool/Archive) without losing bitemporal history; crypto-shred is the terminal erasure. Requires admin wiring to define/manage tier+retention policies and trigger transitions/erasure — ticketed as `specs/03-phase-1-build/03-backend-data-model/11-tiered-data-lifecycle.md`. **Primary driver is scalability + cost** (fully-hydrated raw source material must not sit on hot storage — tiering is what makes raw-first + store-everything affordable at volume); deletion/retention policies are definable **per tier**, not only at terminal erasure. **SUPERSEDED 2026-06-21 (Leo):** the erasure mechanism is the tokenized PII vault (delete-the-row), not crypto-shred — terminal erasure = delete the vault row; tokens elsewhere dereference to nothing. See the PII-erasure-mechanism decision above.

data.statement: - **Raw-first, process close to source, store everything.** Preferred pipeline: raw ingest -> dehydration -> transform -> load -> process -> aggregate. Raw is always preferred; the CDP captures and retains the raw form (bronze) and derives everything downstream. Reaffirms direct-from-source capture (2026-06-12). source.locator: Client-confirmed 2026-06-17 (Dan Aston, Teams chat — open-item reconciliation; DAS spot-checking gaps to inform design/product strategy, more questions incoming)

data.statement: - **Maximize value across ALL sources/channels.** Assume every CDP source and channel is in scope for extracting identity value — identification, heuristics, data retention, model training (later), market data, segmentation, targeting. Document everything per source. Build extractors/adapters for anything DAS does not already ship to us (documented per source). Working scope stance — do not narrow to specific feeds. **This is the deliberate driver of the front-loaded ETL/ingestion engineering investment:** per-source extractor work scales with source count, so ingestion/SSIS-reimplementation is resourced up front (ties to the `phase-1-build.ssis-reimplementation` EPIC and the ETL delivery workflow above). **Cost is contained, though:** Airflow's broad connector/provider ecosystem plus reusable multi-step DAG patterns (raw -> dehydrate -> transform -> load -> process -> aggregate) cover most sources cheaply at low marginal cost per source — bespoke extractor work is only the long-tail of sources lacking an existing connector. The per-source stance is affordable precisely because Airflow does the heavy lifting. The approach is **scalable** (DAG/task parallelism + worker autoscaling), **manageable** (declarative DAGs, connector reuse, two-env PR-tested CI/CD), and **cloud-agnostic** (self-hosted Airflow runs on any Kubernetes — consistent with the agnostic-core decision; no MWAA/ADF lock-in).

The leadership-facing distillation of Phase 0: DAS holds rich customer data across dozens of systems but has no way to recognize one person across them ("we don't" was the answer when asked how identity resolves today), and the legacy join key meant to do it was found all-zero and non-functional. data.detail: Discovery (data source audit, identity landscape, infrastructure inventory) plus the architecture and platform-decision design. Output: this set of deliverables.

Builds the productionized CDP backend (V1) on the portable OSS core, in two sub-phases. 1a — Platform: the full platform ready and tested with one source ingest per channel (the 5 intake primitives — DB / API / SFTP / event / feed) — Foundation, Backend & Data Model, Frontend + read surfaces + search, Identity Resolution + Curation, Segmentation, the Ingest framework, and the Superset reporting baseline. ~4 months (gut-check). MVP is a thin slice inside 1a. 1b — Long-tail migration: onboard all remaining sources, reimplement SSIS, migrate reporting (Juicebox/DWRPT → Superset/warehouse), deprecate legacy. Cloud target is a client choice (Azure-primary preferred, AWS alternative, per the bake-off); the OSS core deploys on either. Infra run-cost: dev baseline ~$1.1k/mo during 1a, prod ~$4.5k/mo phasing in toward 1b (see Detailed Phase 1 & 2 Plans). Workstreams below derive from specs/manifest.json.

data.focus: Applications · Enhancements + Applicatives (can start before 1b at critical data mass)
data.detail: Applications and outbound delivery on the Phase-1 CDP — deliberately able to start before 1b completes, once enough sources are live to be valuable. All infrastructure ships in Phase 1 (segmentation + targeting and the web-UI, the reporting platform, consent + vault erasure, web-UI admin). Two sub-phases. Enhancements: outbound activation & delivery (Meta/TikTok/email/CRM connectors over the Phase-1 NATS backbone, website pixel / JS SDK, event-stream activation); reporting parity (custom-report catalog + self-serve, store-neutral); data exposure & syndication. Applicatives: applications on the CDP — VSS retool (flagship), maintenance/service (CarPlay/mobile), marketing activation, mobile, and data-enrichment — each consuming the golden record / events / consent instead of re-solving identity.

data.focus: AI / ML · 3a External AI → 3b Own ML
